strengths: Establishes a genuinely novel result: an additive (rather than multiplicative) decoupling of the prior-dependent burn-in term from the minimax long-run regret rate for Thompson sampling in the linear-Gaussian bandit, which sharpens a line of prior work (e.g. Kalkanli and Özgür, 2020; Russo and Van Roy, 2014).

The core technical tool, a generalized elliptical potential lemma (Lemma 3) that removes the requirement V0 ⪰ I and allows flexible exponents p ∈ [0,1], is an interesting and potentially independently useful contribution to the bandit-analysis toolkit; the proof technique (Hermitian convexity interpolation, Sherman-Morrison, tight ratio bound via Lemma 5) is nontrivial and carefully executed.

Provides a matching (up to log factors) minimax lower bound (Theorem 6 and its corollaries) that confirms the burn-in term is not an analysis artifact but a real phenomenon, strengthening the claim that the bound is essentially tight.
Extends the main result beyond Gaussian priors/noise to general strongly log-concave distributions (Section 5), broadening applicability somewhat.

Thorough and careful related-work section that explicitly reconciles/decodes implicit scalings in prior work (e.g., showing how bounded-reward or bounded-θ⋆ assumptions in earlier papers implicitly hide ∥θ⋆∥2 dependence), which is valuable for the community's understanding of this literature.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation whatsoever; even simple simulations illustrating the additive vs. multiplicative burn-in behavior (e.g., varying Tr(Σ0) and T) would substantially strengthen the practical relevance and sanity-check the bounds.

The action set is restricted to the canonical ℓ2-ball A ⊂ rB_2^d; while this is standard in some of the cited literature, many practical bandit settings involve more general (e.g., finite, polytope, or context-dependent) action sets, and it is unclear how straightforwardly the results extend.

The lower bound (Theorem 6/Corollaries 7-8) is explicitly acknowledged not to exactly match the instance-specific upper bound in general, only for 'non-pathological' (e.g., polynomially-scaling eigenvalue) priors; the gap for general Σ0 is not fully characterized, leaving some looseness in the claimed tightness.

The generalization in Section 5 is deferred essentially entirely to the appendix with the claim it follows 'mutatis mutandis,' but the concentration argument there (via sub-Gaussianity of log-concave posteriors and Orlicz-norm chaining) is more involved than a trivial adaptation, and its correctness is hard for a reader to verify without carefully working through the appendix.

Comparisons to very recent related work (Zhang et al., 2025) suggest overlapping insights in the zero-noise/deterministic-feedback regime, somewhat narrowing the perceived novelty of the burn-in-necessity claim, though the current paper's noisy setting and tighter constants are a distinguishing factor.

The presentation, while organized, is very dense with many constants (C1, C2) and multi-step derivations; a high-level intuition or sketch earlier in the paper (before the full proof) for why the decoupling should hold would improve accessibility.

strengths: The paper achieves a genuinely novel result: an additive (rather than multiplicative) separation of the prior-diffusiveness 'burn-in' term from the minimax σd√T rate in Thompson sampling regret for linear-Gaussian bandits, a cleaner and more interpretable characterization than prior work (e.g., Kalkanli and Özgür, 2020).

The generalized elliptical potential lemma (Lemma 3) is a nontrivial technical contribution: it removes the standard requirement that V0 ⪰ I and introduces a flexible exponent p, together with a careful Hermitian-convexity interpolation argument (via Lewis, 1996) and a Hölder-based lemma (Lemma 5) to control the transition regime. This tool appears reusable beyond the specific application in this paper.

The paper provides a matching (up to log factors) minimax lower bound (Theorem 6, Corollaries 7-8) adapting Rusmevichientong and Tsitsiklis (2010), which substantiates that the burn-in term is not an artifact of loose analysis but a fundamental feature of the problem.

The related work section is unusually careful and thorough, explicitly identifying subtle implicit dependencies on ∥θ⋆∥2 hidden in several prior papers' bounds (Abeille and Lazaric, Agrawal and Goyal, Dong and Van Roy, Hamidi and Bayati, Russo and Van Roy), which strengthens the paper's positioning and shows deep familiarity with the literature.
The extension to strongly log-concave priors and noise (Section 5) demonstrates that the technique is not narrowly tied to Gaussianity, broadening applicability somewhat.
weaknesses: The paper contains zero empirical validation. For a paper whose central claims concern the practical behavior of Thompson sampling regret (burn-in vs. long-run rate), even simple synthetic simulations illustrating the additive decoupling phenomenon and the tightness of the bounds would substantially strengthen confidence in the practical relevance of the result; as is, the contribution is purely theoretical with no sanity check.

The main theorem is restricted to the canonical setting where the action set is exactly (or a subset of) the ℓ2-ball of radius r; general compact/convex/finite action sets (which are standard and often more practically relevant, e.g., finite-armed linear bandits) are not covered, limiting the scope of the claimed improvement relative to a substantial swath of the literature it compares against.

The authors themselves acknowledge that the lower bound does not achieve an instance-specific match with the upper bound; the matching is only established for essentially two special cases (scaled-identity and 'polynomially-decaying' eigenvalue priors), so the claim that the burn-in term is 'unavoidable' is not fully general and leaves open whether the upper bound is loose for other covariance structures.

The overall improvement, while conceptually appealing (additive vs. multiplicative coupling), yields limited quantitative gain in many parameter regimes; the paper's own discussion notes Thompson sampling is 'near-optimal' only when T ≤ r²Tr(Σ0)/σ², i.e., the sharper characterization matters primarily in a bounded regime of T, somewhat tempering the significance of the improvement.

The presentation is dense and reference-heavy in places (e.g., the terse enumeration of related work, heavy notational overhead with C1, C2, multiple constants), which could be streamlined; some steps (e.g., justification for specific constants like '24 log T' or choices of s in the concentration argument) are asserted without much intuition-building for a broader ICML audience.

The generalization to log-concave distributions in Section 5, while a nice addition, is somewhat mechanically derived via sub-Gaussian concentration arguments and does not provide fundamentally new insight beyond the Gaussian case; its practical significance (e.g., which log-concave noise/prior combinations arise in applications) is not discussed.

strengths: The paper resolves a genuine gap in the literature: previous regret bounds for Thompson sampling in the linear-Gaussian bandit (e.g., Kalkanli and Özgür, 2020) exhibit a multiplicative dependence between the prior diffusiveness term and the minimax rate, and this paper shows the two terms decouple additively, which is a meaningful sharpening.

The central technical tool, the generalized elliptical potential lemma (Lemma 3), is a nontrivial and reusable generalization of the standard elliptical potential lemma: it removes the requirement that V0 be at least the identity and introduces a flexible exponent p, with a clean interpolation-based proof using convexity of the Hermitian trace-power function. This appears to be a contribution of independent interest to the broader bandit literature.

The paper backs its upper bound with a matching lower bound (Theorem 6 and Corollaries 7-8), establishing that the burn-in term drβˆš(Tr Σ0) is generally unavoidable, at least up to logarithmic factors for non-pathological (scaled-identity or polynomially-decaying) priors, which strengthens the claim that the new bound is 'correct' rather than merely an improvement.

The related work section carefully audits several existing analyses (Abeille & Lazaric, Agrawal & Goyal, Dong & Van Roy, Hamidi & Bayati, Russo & Van Roy variants) and explicitly identifies implicit dependence on the scale of θ⋆ hidden in boundedness assumptions, which is a useful clarifying contribution to the field beyond the new bound itself.

Section 5 generalizes the main result to strongly log-concave priors and noise distributions (not necessarily Gaussian), broadening the applicability of the technique and demonstrating that the elliptical-potential-based proof strategy is not tied to Gaussian conjugacy.

The proofs are presented in reasonably complete and checkable detail, including auxiliary lemmas (e.g., sub-Gaussianity of log-concave distributions, Orlicz-norm concentration) with self-contained derivations in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation; while this may be acceptable for a theory contribution, some simulations verifying the additive burn-in phenomenon (e.g., comparing empirical regret curves against the multiplicative vs. additive bounds across a range of prior diffusiveness values) would substantially strengthen the practical relevance and provide a sanity check on the proof mechanics.

The results are restricted to the canonical action set A ⊂ rB_2^d (the scaled Euclidean ball). Many practically relevant bandit settings use finite action sets, polytopes, or context-dependent action sets, and it is unclear how readily the elliptical potential machinery extends to these cases, which somewhat limits the scope of significance claimed.

The lower bound in Theorem 6/Corollaries 7-8 matches the upper bound only for specific 'non-pathological' prior spectra (scaled identity or polynomial eigenvalue decay); the paper does not provide an instance-wise matching lower bound for general Σ0, which is acknowledged but leaves open whether the drβˆš(Tr Σ0) upper bound is tight in all regimes (e.g., very skewed spectra).

The presentation is dense and notation-heavy even relative to typical bandit theory papers (multiple constants C1, C2, several nested lemma dependencies), which could be streamlined with more intuition-building text or a roadmap figure to aid readers less steeped in this specific literature.

The interpretation of the burn-in term given in the proof of Corollary 2 ('the regret incurred by a very suboptimal action is on the order of rβˆš(Tr(Σ0))') is somewhat informal and could be tightened into a more rigorous heuristic argument or removed if not load-bearing.

The generalization to strongly log-concave distributions in Section 5 assumes the noise is strongly log-concave on R (scalar) while the prior is strongly log-concave in R^d; it would help to discuss concrete non-Gaussian examples satisfying these assumptions to clarify the practical scope of this generalization.
